source.title: Beyond Task Performance: Evaluating and Reducing the Flaws of Large Multimodal Models with In-Context Learning
source.authors: Mustafa Shukor; Alexandre Ramé; Corentin Dancette; M. Cord

record.tranche_reason: The study compares multimodal model performance across sizes on downstream benchmarks, rather than measuring held-out language-model loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, predict larger runs from smaller runs, or optimize parameter-token allocations. It does report its own comparisons of model size and downstream abilities, which bear on V6. Results cited from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study compares its own downstream results across 10 off-the-shelf image-text LMMs (3B–80B), which bears loosely on V6 in a new setting. Size is confounded with training data, LLM initialization and instruction tuning. There are no loss measurements or quantitative fits, so predictability itself is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that LMMs (3B–80B) have flaws in hallucination, abstention, compositionality, explainability and instruction following that 'remain unsolved with scaling alone'. Larger size helps abstention (up to 9B) and explanations. ICL helps some flaws, does nothing for compositionality, and amplifies hallucination. They do not attribute the 80B explanation exception to size; that remark concerns instruction tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream multimodal abilities across existing model variants; it does not measure language-model loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies by ability and benchmark; explanation quality has an 80B exception, and compositionality conclusions differ between CREPE and SugarCREPE.

fits_no_version.finding: ICL amplifies hallucination more for smaller models (<9B); IDEFICS-80B suffers less from the amplification.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model scale moderates how in-context demonstrations change downstream failure behaviour in LMMs.

record.problems: Size comparisons span models with differing training data, language-model initialization, and instruction tuning, so they are not controlled scaling sweeps. The study reports no pretraining-loss results or quantitative scaling fits. Some relevant trends are stated in text or figures without numerical values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant version-6 size-trend result was left out. Results about ICL shot counts and proposed ICL variants were not included because they do not test the effect of model scale.

untested.parts: Predictability (quantitative fit or extrapolation) of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; controlled size sweeps with fixed data and initialization.
All: no extrapolation from fitted laws.
All: no shape ablations at fixed parameters.
No power-law fits in the image-text setting; the remarks on other modalities are argument only.
All: no fits or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Per-model zero-shot CHAIRs and CIDEr values, which show no monotone size trend.
Per-size abstention F1 and explanation CIDEr numbers behind the stated size trends.
missing.locator: Figure 2b, Figure 4 (values only in figures); Tables 5–7 for 9B models

record.verdict_notes: All size comparisons span models differing in training data, LLM backbone and instruction tuning, so they are weak evidence on V6. The appendix even says 'we only consider models up to 9B', which contradicts the 80B evaluations elsewhere. The abstract's 'scaling alone' statement leans on comparisons with smaller finetuned specialist models.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute; power-law form and bottleneck conditions.
Predictions of larger-run loss from power laws fitted to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling with compute.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates image-text models; its comments about other modalities do not report experimental results on them or on the other listed training regimes.
It compares downstream abilities across model sizes, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss or follows a quantitative scaling law.
The study does not compare fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: OFv2-3B, OFv2-4B, OFv1-9B
rows.operation_detail: Compared abstention performance across model sizes.
rows.value: Increasing model size up to 9B improves abstention.
rows.note: The reported comparison is across model variants; the study also discusses differences in data and training.
rows.check: State is fine, but the comparison is confounded: OFv1-9B was trained on less data than the OFv2 models. 'Up to certain scale (9B)' implies the trend is not claimed beyond 9B. The value comes from figure text only, with no numbers.

rows.subject: LMMs (models compared)
rows.operation_detail: Compared explanation quality across model sizes.
rows.value: The authors report a clear positive correlation between model size and explanation quality, with an exception for 80B models.
rows.note: The text describes the trend but does not provide the comparison values here.
rows.check: The 80B exception belongs to a separate sentence about instruction tuning and LLM unfreezing, not the size trend (see r3). Within 3B–9B the authors report a clear positive size–explanation correlation, so the state should be observed, not partial. Size range should read roughly 3B–9B, plus IDEFICS-80B, which surpasses SoTA with ICL.

rows.subject: IDEFICS-80B
rows.operation_detail: Compared explanation quality with the size trend reported for other models.
rows.value: The positive size correlation reported for other models does not hold for 80B models; the authors suggest possible overfitting when training the language model.
rows.note: This is the study's stated exception to the size trend.
rows.check: Misread. The text first credits better data and instruction tuning with the LLM unfrozen, then adds 'for 80B-parameter models this is not the case… overfitting when training the LLM'. This refers to instruction tuning failing to help at 80B (IDEFICS-80B vs 80B (I)), not to model size failing to help. IDEFICS-80B is described as the best explainer with ICL. The row is not a size result.

rows.subject: LMMs (models compared)
rows.operation_detail: Compared compositionality performance across models and sizes.
rows.baseline: Random chance is the stated reference for CREPE; no numeric reference stated for SugarCREPE.
rows.value: Models are described as close to random on the evaluated categories despite scaling parameters and training examples. The apparent advantage of 80B models on CREPE may reflect benchmark biases; all LMMs perform poorly on SugarCREPE.
rows.note: The authors caution that CREPE's apparent large-model improvement may come from dataset biases rather than improved compositionality.
rows.check: State is acceptable. The finding is stated qualitatively from Figures 3 and 7 with no per-size numbers. The 80B gain on CREPE is attributed to benchmark bias, and all LMMs are poor on SugarCREPE.

rows.subject: LMMs (models compared)
rows.operation_detail: Compared object hallucination across model sizes.
rows.measure: Object hallucination rate measured by CHAIRs
rows.value: The authors state that scaling LMMs alone is not enough to reduce hallucinations.
rows.note: The text also identifies more multimodal pretraining data and unfreezing language-model weights as factors associated with reduced hallucination.
rows.check: The authors' 'scaling is not enough' rests mainly on LMMs versus smaller COCO-finetuned captioners, not on a within-LMM size sweep. Across LMM sizes, Table 4 zero-shot CHAIRs shows no monotone decrease: OFv2-3B 6.85, OFv2-4B 8.35, OFv2-9B 7.21, IDEFICS-9B 31.42. Absent fits better than partial.

relationships.condition: Abstention (TDIUC) and explanation quality (VQA-X) across confounded OF/IDEFICS models from 3B to 9B
relationships.reason: Authors report abstention and explanation quality improving with model size (r1, r2). The comparison is not a controlled sweep and gives no predictive fit.
relationships.display_finding: Abstention and explanation quality improved with model size, although the comparison was uncontrolled and provided no predictive fit.

relationships.condition: Compositionality on bias-reduced SugarCREPE (and CREPE HN-Atom), 3B–80B
relationships.reason: Models stay near chance despite scale; the 80B CREPE gain is attributed to benchmark bias (r4).
relationships.display_finding: Performance stayed near chance from 3B to 80B, and the authors attributed the 80B CREPE gain to benchmark bias.

relationships.condition: Object hallucination (CHAIRs, zero-shot COCO) across LMM sizes
relationships.reason: No size trend in CHAIRs (Table 4: 3B 6.85, 4B 8.35, 9B 7.21); larger LMMs still hallucinate more than smaller finetuned captioners (r5).
relationships.display_finding: CHAIRs scores were 6.85, 8.35, and 7.21 at 3B, 4B, and 9B, and larger models hallucinated more than smaller fine-tuned captioners.
